mcqs.question: How do display: none and visibility: hidden differ in terms of the render tree?
options: Both display:none and visibility:hidden elements are excluded from the render tree
visibility:hidden elements are excluded from the render tree, but display:none elements are not
display:none elements are excluded from the render tree entirely, while visibility:hidden ones remain in it but simply aren't painted
Neither is excluded from the render tree; both are only skipped during the paint stage
mcqs.explanation: display:none removes the element and its subtree from the render tree, so it doesn't occupy layout space at all. visibility:hidden keeps the box in layout and in the render tree — it's just not painted — which is why toggling it is cheaper to animate.

mcqs.question: You add box-shadow to a large number of list items and paint time spikes in DevTools. Why is this heavier than it looks?
options: box-shadow triggers a network request to resolve the blur rendering
box-shadow disables GPU compositing entirely for the whole page
box-shadow changes only affect the CSSOM, never paint
Each shadow is a nontrivial rasterization operation per element, so paint cost scales with element count and shadow complexity, not just visible area
mcqs.explanation: Paint cost isn't just proportional to pixels covered — effects like shadows and rounded corners are comparatively expensive per element to rasterize, so a long list with per-item shadows adds up fast. Nothing about box-shadow touches the network or disables compositing.

mcqs.question: Why does animating transform typically stay smooth even when the main thread is busy with other JS, while animating width does not?
options: transform changes can be handled entirely by the compositor thread on an existing layer, skipping layout and paint; width changes force layout on the main thread every frame
width changes are inherently slower because width is measured in pixels rather than percentages
transform changes are rendered by the network process instead of the renderer
Browsers automatically cache every transform value, unlike width
mcqs.explanation: A transform on a composited layer only needs the compositor thread to recombine already-painted bitmaps, bypassing the main thread entirely. A width change invalidates geometry, so it forces layout (and usually paint) on the main thread before compositing can even happen.

mcqs.question: Which of these CSS changes requires the full render tree, layout, paint, and composite chain, with no available shortcut?
options: Changing an element's color
Changing an element's opacity
Changing an element's transform: translateX
Changing an element's width
mcqs.explanation: Width affects geometry, so it invalidates layout and everything downstream of it. Color skips layout but still needs a repaint; opacity and transform can often be handled by the compositor alone, skipping both layout and paint.

mcqs.question: A CSS <link> in <head> is render-blocking. Does it also block HTML parsing?
options: Yes — CSS always halts tokenization until the stylesheet is fully downloaded
No — the HTML parser keeps tokenizing past the link tag; it's the render tree, which needs the completed CSSOM, that has to wait
Only if the stylesheet contains @import rules
Only on a page's very first load, not on repeat visits
mcqs.explanation: Render-blocking and parser-blocking are separate effects: CSS holds up the render tree (and therefore first paint) but doesn't pause HTML tokenization, unlike a synchronous script which blocks both.

mcqs.question: A CSS-in-JS library injects a <style> tag on component mount, after first paint. What production symptom does this most directly cause?
options: A memory leak in the renderer process
A CORS error on the stylesheet request
Cumulative Layout Shift, since already-painted content has its styles changed and gets re-laid-out after the user has already seen it
A permanent block on the JS engine's JIT compiler
mcqs.explanation: Styles injected after first paint force a late layout/paint recalculation on content the user has already seen, which is exactly what Cumulative Layout Shift measures. It has no direct relationship to memory leaks, CORS, or JIT behavior.
